analysis.title: Global Macro Chart of the Day (#192): Searching for AI in the productivity data
key_insights: UBS finds AI is not yet visible in productivity data. The essay is in the Global Economics & Markets Outlook 2027/2028.
US labour productivity growth averaged 1.6% in 2004-19 and 2.4% in 2023-26, but has slipped to 2.1% over the last four quarters. The deviation from the pre-pandemic trend is modest.

In 41 of 47 economies studied (the US plus 46 others), the deviation from the pre-pandemic productivity trend is smaller than in the US. Only five show a larger pick-up and only Taiwan clearly stands out.

UBS forecasts Taiwan's growth at 12.5% this year, largely because Taiwan is a key AI supplier and receives a large share of US hyperscaler capex. Taiwan's high profits add directly to GDP, which raises output per worker. UBS calls this a measurement effect, not firms having learned to use AI.
UBS attributes only about 5% of the US productivity pick-up to greater AI use. Enterprise adoption is in the low 20s percent and agentic AI has barely been rolled out.
AI implementation spending is concentrated, with 2% of firms accounting for half of the total. Executives who say they have adopted AI report usage of a few hours a week on average.

In past episodes such as the 1990s, capital deepening led productivity gains by around three years. UBS says the current AI cycle is in that phase, and training, integration and workflow redesign still have to happen before measurable impacts appear.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Down from the 2.4% average in 2023-26 and above the 1.6% average in 2004-19. The pick-up versus the pre-pandemic trend is modest, and UBS attributes about 5% of it to AI.
Above the 2004-19 average of 1.6%, but UBS says it is hard to link this to AI use.
Pre-pandemic baseline for the trend comparison.
UBS forecast. It reflects Taiwan's role as an AI supplier and its share of US hyperscaler capex. Output divided by workers raises measured productivity without firms having adopted AI.

risk_factors: Productivity gains from AI may take longer to appear because adoption is shallow, spending is concentrated and agentic AI has barely been rolled out.
Taiwan's productivity jump is a measurement effect from AI-supplier profits and hyperscaler capex, so it is not evidence of AI adoption gains and depends on continued capex.

tension_points.bull_case: Past episodes such as the 1990s show capital deepening leading productivity gains by around three years, and the economy is in that phase now. Training, integration and workflow redesign should eventually produce measurable gains.
tension_points.bear_case: Only about 5% of the US productivity pick-up is attributable to AI, enterprise adoption is in the low 20s percent, usage averages a few hours a week and spending is concentrated in 2% of firms.

theme_stances.key_argument: It is too early in adoption to expect productivity gains from AI, and only about 5% of the US pick-up is attributable to it.
theme_stances.evidence: it is too early in adoption to expect productivity gains
